content: In nuclear physics, a decay product, also referred to as a daughter product, daughter isotope, or daughter nuclide, is a nuclide that results from the radioactive decay of a parent isotope or precursor nuclide. The daughter product may either be stable or undergo further decay to form its own daughter product. In cases where the daughter product itself decays, the resulting nuclide is sometimes called a granddaughter product. Decay products play a critical role in understanding radioactive decay processes and in the management of radioactive waste. Practically speaking, nearly all decay products are themselves radioactive. This leads to the formation of decay chains rather than a single decay product, with the chain eventually terminating in a stable nuclide. For elements with atomic numbers higher than lead, the stable endpoint of the decay chain is almost always an isotope of lead. Lead generally represents the stable point at which decay chains cease. In many instances, members of a decay chain are significantly more radioactive than the original nuclide. For example, while pure uranium is not highly radioactive, certain samples of naturally occurring pitchblende can be quite hazardous due to their radium content. Similarly, thorium gas mantles exhibit very low levels of radioactivity when new, but their radioactivity increases substantially after just a few months of storage. Although it is impossible to predict the exact moment when a specific atom of a radioactive substance will decay, the decay products of a radioactive substance are highly predictable. This predictability makes decay products invaluable to scientists across various fields who need to determine the quantity or type of the parent product. Such studies are often conducted to measure pollution levels, particularly in and around nuclear facilities, as well as for other scientific and environmental purposes.
